schemaVersion: Ehel Intensive English Course Plan v1.0
subject: English
audience: Adult ESL learners of any first language, beginner upwards, studying intensively and mostly alone. No child-world, and no task that assumes a particular adult life (a job, a car, a home, children or papers): where a task needs one, the learner may invent it.
designModel: Grade 1 English: full-screen pattern carousel, one idea per screen, audio on every line. Level 1 Unit 0 teaches the letters and the course's instruction words.

cefr.name: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
cefr.role: Defines what a learner can DO at the end of each level, and therefore what each level's exit assessment tests. This is the framework the course reports against.
cefr.structure: Three levels, and the course ENDS at B1. Level 1 (0057 Stages 1-3) runs Pre-A1 to A1, Level 2 (0057 Stages 4-6) A1 to A2, and Level 3 (0876 Stages 7-9) A2 to B1. Each opens where the one below it exits, which is the property the 2026-09-12 rebuild existed to restore — before it, Level 1 exited at A1 and Level 2 opened at B1, so nothing taught the two levels between them. See whyTheCourseStopsAtB1.

cambridge.name: Cambridge Primary English as a Second Language 0057; Cambridge Primary English 0058; Cambridge Lower Secondary English 0861
cambridge.role: 0057 is the CONTRACT for Levels 1 and 2: every 0057 objective of a level's stages is placed in exactly one unit (plan field `esl`), and the build fails a unit whose outcomes do not cite its placed objectives. 0058 is an optional literacy cross-reference. Level 3 and above keep the 0058 / 0861 codes of the school units they were compressed from.

frameworks.howTheyRelate: They are not the same axis. A Cambridge stage supplies the language sequence; CEFR sets the target and is recorded separately for each skill as a language-support measure. Level 1 follows the owner's planning note (Stages 1-3, Pre-A1 to A1) and Level 2 will follow Stages 4-6 (A1 to A2). Completing a level does not by itself establish a CEFR level: reading, writing, listening and speaking are assessed separately and may be at different levels.

sourceMaterial: src/prototypes/ehel-academy/english/grade-{1..8} — 81 units, 2212 vocabulary items, 486 grammar lessons. Analysis: inputs/ehel-english-intensive-source/grade-1-8-analysis.json
compressionPrinciple: Grades 1-8 teach 16 language patterns more than once, because children need spiral return. Adults do not. Each pattern is taught ONCE here, at the point it first becomes useful, and then recycled through later units' tasks rather than re-taught. That is where the 81-to-40 compression comes from — not from cutting language. A card that CONTRASTS patterns already taught is not a re-teach, but it must be flagged with "contrast": true so the duplication gate can allow it explicitly rather than by accident.
whatIsDropped: Child-world topics with no adult use (Fun and Games, All About Bugs, animal sounds, costumes) — their grammar is kept, their topic is replaced with an adult context that carries the same pattern.
Repeat teaching of a pattern already taught. The second and third pass become practice inside a later unit, not a grammar lesson.
Per-grade capstones (five of them across grades 1-4, five across 5-8) collapse into one capstone per level.

Whole-alphabet phonics. Adult learners arrive already literate in some script and mostly decoding Latin letters. Unit 0 teaches the sounds and syllable shapes that are hard in English, and lets the learner find out by testing themselves which of those are hard for them.

levels.label: Phonics — Reading the Sounds
levels.cefrName: Pre-A1, before any English at all
levels._whyBelowIntro: Intro assumes a learner can hold a pen and that letters have names. This level assumes neither. It is Cambridge Primary English Phonics Workbooks A and B, combined and rebuilt for adults: the sounds first, the letters that spell them second, blending them into words third. It claims no Cambridge 0057 objective for the same reason Intro does not.

cefrBands.cefrName: Pre-A1, before any English at all
cefrBands.canDo: Hear the separate sounds in a short word, know a letter for each of them, blend them to read a word, and write a word from the sounds you can hear in it.

levels.exitDescriptor: Exits ready for Intro Unit 1. Can read and write short regular words sound by sound, read the commonest irregular words by sight, and read a simple sentence aloud.
levels.exitAssessment: A reading check at the end of Unit 20: ten regular words, five common irregular words and one sentence, read aloud. Not a barrier — Intro re-teaches the letters and Level 1 Unit 0 teaches them a third time.

levels.label: Intro — Starting English
levels.cefrName: Pre-A1, from no English at all
levels._whyNoEslFramework: Cambridge 0057 has no stage below Stage 1, and all 42 Stage 1 objectives are placed in Level 1. The build's coverage gate is per level and total, so a level declaring Stage 1 must cite every one of them — which would make Intro a second copy of Level 1's first third. Intro is below the framework, not inside it, and cites 0058 Stage 1 for the literacy it does deliver.

cefrBands.cefrName: Pre-A1, from no English at all
cefrBands.canDo: Understand and say greetings, your own name, numbers and the words for people, things and places around you; copy the 26 letters and begin to read short familiar words.

levels.exitDescriptor: Exits ready for Level 1 Unit 0. Can hold a pen and copy the 26 letters in both forms, say the alphabet, spell their own name, count to twenty, and ask and answer about people, things, places, food, health and work in two- and three-word turns. Begins to blend sounds into short words.
levels.exitAssessment: A Pre-A1 check at the end of Unit 16, reported per skill and never as one grade. It is not a barrier: Level 1 Unit 0 re-teaches the letters and blending, so a learner may move on before passing it.

the seven days

levels.label: Level 1 — Foundation

cefrBands.canDo: Recognise familiar words and letters, follow simple instructions with support, and introduce yourself with rehearsed words and phrases.
Ask and answer basic questions, read short sentences, and write simple personal information.
Understand short familiar texts, and describe people, places, routines and events using simple sentences.

levels.exitDescriptor: Exits at a secure A1. Can recognise and write the letters, read and understand short familiar texts, ask and answer simple questions about people, places, routines and events, follow and give simple instructions, and write short sentences and notes joined with and, but and because.
levels.exitAssessment: A1 check across the four skills at the end of Unit 19, reported per skill, never as one grade. Passing it is the entry condition for Level 2.

units.title: Letters and Sounds
units.context: The alphabet, letter names and sounds, reading a short word by blending its sounds, and the instruction words every later unit uses.
patterns: the 26 letters: their names, capital and small forms, and alphabetical order
short vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u
consonant sounds, including sh, ch and th
blending: reading a short word sound by sound (b-u-s, bus)
the course's instruction words: listen, look, say, read, write, tap, match, check
units.note: Letters ARE taught now: 0057 Stage 1 puts letter names, letter sounds, blending and left-to-right writing in scope (1Rd.01, 1Rd.02, 1Wca.01, 1Wca.02). A learner who already reads the Latin alphabet can check themselves in the first screen and move to Unit 1. Every explanation in this unit must work through sound, a picture and a very short line; the learner may have no English yet.

units.title: Hello, My Name Is
units.context: Greeting people, saying who you are and where you are from, spelling your name, and numbers to twenty.
patterns: am, is, are: saying who someone is (I am Ana. She is from a small town.)
I, you, he, she, it, we, they
first question words: what, who, where, how old
numbers 1 to 20

units.title: My Family, My Things
units.context: The people in a family and the everyday things you carry.
patterns: my, your, his, her, our, their
a and the
this and these
one thing, two things: plural -s

units.title: Colours and Where Things Are
units.context: Colours, simple describing words, and where things are in a room.
patterns: colour words and describing words before a noun: a red bag, a big box
it is and it has: saying what a thing is and has
in, on, at, near, next to: where things are
here and there

units.title: I Can, I Like
units.context: What people can and cannot do, and what they like doing.
patterns: can and can't: saying what you are able to do
like + -ing: I like cooking. I don't like running.
and: joining two words or two ideas
units.note: Replace the source's Fun and Games framing (toys, playground) with things any age does: cook, drive, swim, sing, speak a language.

units.title: What Is Happening Now
units.context: What people are doing at this moment, at home, at school or work, and in the street; asking someone to help you understand.
patterns: am, is, are + -ing: saying what is happening now
not + -ing: saying what is not happening
questions and short answers: Are you working? Yes, I am.

units.title: Days, Dates and Time
units.context: Days of the week, first to tenth, times of the day, and doing things with people and for people. Ends with the Stage 1 check.
patterns: first, second, third … tenth
on and in for time: on Monday, in the morning
with and for: with a friend, for my sister
units.note: Stage 1 checkpoint: the unit's quiz and assignment revisit Units 0-6 as well as this unit's patterns.

units.title: Asking and Answering
units.context: Finding out about people: where they live, what job they do, how to spell a name.
patterns: do and does in questions: Do you live here? Where does she work?
short answers: Yes, I do. No, she doesn't.
short forms: I'm, don't, doesn't, isn't
you meaning anyone: How do you spell that?

units.title: There Is, There Are
units.context: Food and the kitchen: what there is at home, and whose things are whose.
patterns: there is and there are
things you can count and things you cannot: an apple, some rice; child and children
possessive 's: Sara's bag
this, that, these, those, and one: the red one
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs

units.title: Numbers to 100, and How Things Are
units.context: Prices and numbers to a hundred, dates, describing people, how people do things, and adding information with too.
patterns: numbers 21 to 100
first to fiftieth: dates like the 21st
-ly words for how you do something: quickly, carefully
too: I like it too
describing words for people and things
my, your, his, her … to describe familiar things

units.title: Yesterday
units.context: What you did yesterday, last week and last month; reading a short story with confidence.
patterns: past with -ed: worked, played, stopped
common irregular past forms: went, had, saw, ate, got
did in questions and not: Did you go? I didn't go.
yesterday, today, last week: words for a definite time

vocabulary.title: Doing words with new past forms

units.title: Can I? I Will
units.context: Asking for things and asking permission, promising and offering, clock times, and travel: tickets, trains and taxis.
patterns: Can I…? Can you…? to ask and to ask permission, with answers: here you are, OK, sure
will for what you mean to do: I'll call you.
at for clock times: at six o'clock, at night
-ing questions with short answers and short forms: Are you coming? Yes, I am.

units.title: Where Things Go
units.context: Places in a town, where things are and where they go, what you use to do a job, and how you feel.
patterns: behind, between, in front of, to: where things are and where they go
with for the thing you use, for for the person who gets it: cut it with a knife, a present for you
saying how you feel: I'm tired. I feel happy.

units.title: Joining and Writing Sentences
units.context: Writing short notes, lists and postcards; joining ideas with but, or and then; capital letters and punctuation. Ends with the Stage 2 check.
patterns: but, or and then: joining words and ideas
capital letters: names, places, days and the start of a sentence
full stops and question marks
planning, writing and checking a short text
units.note: Stage 2 checkpoint: the unit's quiz and assignment revisit Units 7-13.

units.title: Every Day
units.context: Routines, habits and states: what usually happens and what is happening now.
patterns: present simple for routines: I get up at six. She works in a shop.
present simple or -ing: I work here. I am working now.
how often: always, usually, often, sometimes, never
state verbs: want, need, know, prefer

units.title: Do This, Then That
units.context: Instructions and directions: following a recipe, finding a place, reading a sign.
patterns: instructions: Turn left. Mix the flour.
first, next, then, after that, finally
left, right, straight on
above, below, inside, opposite, outside, under

units.title: What Happened
units.context: Telling what happened on a day, a trip or in bad weather, in the right order.
patterns: the past to tell events in order: I got up, had breakfast and left.
was, were, and more irregular past forms: came, told, felt, thought
before and after: after lunch, before work
last night, two days ago, at the weekend
him, her, them, it in a story; gave him the keys

units.title: Bigger, Better, More
units.context: Comparing places, prices and things; how much and how many; numbers to a thousand.
patterns: -er and more: cheaper, more expensive; the -est and the most
good, better, best; bad, worse, worst
how you do it: quietly, well, hard, badly
some, any, many, much, a lot of, no
this one, that one: Which one is yours?
numbers to 1,000

units.title: Have You Ever? Shall We?
units.context: Experiences, suggestions and plans, rules, and what you could do in the past; places in nature.
patterns: Have you ever…? I have… I have never…: talking about experiences
Shall we…? to suggest; Will you…? to ask about plans
must for what is necessary
could for what you were able to do in the past
more question forms: What kind of…? How long…? How far…?

units.title: Because, and To
units.context: Giving reasons and purposes, hopes and decisions, how and with whom you travel; bringing Level 1 together in a portfolio and the Level 1 check.
patterns: because: giving a reason
to + verb for a purpose: I went to the shop to buy bread.
verb + to or -ing: I hope to…, I enjoy -ing
by, with, from, without: by bus, from the city, without sugar
units.note: Level 1 capstone. The assignment is a portfolio from at least four units plus recordings, and the unit closes with the Level 1 check across the four skills, reported per skill.

levels.label: Level 2 — Independence

cefrBands.canDo: Talk about your own routine and your own past in more than one sentence, say what you have done and what you still have to do, and follow a short set of instructions.
Say how long something has been true, give an opinion and a reason for it, explain how something works, and tell a longer story about the past.
Keep a conversation going, pass on what somebody else said, describe how a thing is made, give advice, and write a connected account of something that took time.

levels.exitDescriptor: Exits at a secure A2. Can describe a routine, an experience and a past event in connected sentences, say how long something has been true, explain how something works, report what somebody said, give and take advice, talk about what will happen if something else does, and write a short connected text with the parts joined and punctuated.
levels.exitAssessment: A2 check across the four skills at the end of Unit 20, reported per skill and never as one grade. Passing it is the entry condition for Level 3.

units.title: Your Week, Your Work
units.context: Describing your own week in detail: what you do, what you need to do, and what you think of it.
patterns: the irregular he, she and it forms: he does, she has, it goes
something, anything, nothing: a thing you do not name
like for describing and about for the subject: What is it like? A book about money.
I need to go, I finish working: which verb takes which

units.title: Offers, Instructions and Checking
units.context: Being a host and being a guest: offering, inviting, giving someone a short set of instructions, and checking you have understood.
patterns: the short question on the end: You work here, don't you? It isn't far, is it?
would you like + a thing to offer and would you like + a verb to invite, with yes please and no thank you
positive and negative instructions in a sequence: Put it here. Don't press that yet.

units.title: Already, Yet, Ever
units.context: What you have done and what you have not done yet: a list of errands, forms and appointments you are working through.
patterns: have and has + the past form, for something finished at no stated time: I have posted it.
yet, already and still: where they go in the line
putting the time part first: Before I leave, I look at the list.

units.title: Plans and Predictions
units.context: Arranging what happens next: what is already fixed, what you have decided, and what you only think will happen.
patterns: am, is, are + -ing for a fixed arrangement: I am meeting her on Tuesday.
be going to for a decision already made, and will for a guess: It is going to rain. I think it will be fine.
to + verb to say why you are doing it: I am going early to get a seat.

units.title: While It Was Happening
units.context: An ordinary day that did not go to plan: what happened, and what was going on around it.
patterns: the past for a habit you had and a state you were in: I worked there for two years.
was and were + -ing for the background: I was waiting when the call came.
then, and after that: carrying an account forward

units.title: How Much, How Many, Which Way
units.context: Buying what you need and finding your way to it: how much of a thing, and which direction.
patterns: a few people, a little water: which word goes with which kind of noun
each and every: each box, every day
into, out of, from, towards, along, across: which way a thing goes

units.title: Better, Worse, and What I Have To Do
units.context: Choosing between two options and saying what you must do about it: rules, what is necessary, and what is only possible.
patterns: more and the most for the longer words: more useful, the most careful
more slowly, the most carefully: comparing the way a thing is done
have to and had to for what you cannot avoid; might, may and could for what is merely possible
who, which and that to say WHICH one you mean: the woman who fixed it

vocabulary.title: Rules and what you must do

units.note: 4Rd.04 says word roots and derivations “including links to words in their first language”. This course is language-neutral and monolingual: teach the roots and the word families in English only — care, careful, careless, carefully — and never ask the learner about another language. Last unit of Stage 4, so it is a checkpoint.

units.title: For and Since
units.context: How long something has been true: a home, a job, a habit, a health matter that is still going on.
patterns: for and since: how long a thing has been true, and still is
how long questions and the answers to them: How long have you had it?
somebody, everywhere, no one: a person or a place you do not name

units.title: Boring or Bored
units.context: Saying how a thing is, how it makes you feel, and how much of that quality there is.
patterns: -ing and -ed describing words: the work is tiring, and I am tired
size, age, then material: the order they go in
too, not enough, quite and rather: how much of a quality there is
good at, interested in, afraid of: the word that always follows

units.title: I Think, I Hope, I Am Sure
units.context: Giving an opinion and asking for something politely: what you think, what you would like, and what is not allowed.
patterns: I think, I know, I hope, I am sure + a whole sentence: I think it closes at five.
so and when to join two ideas inside a short text
mustn't for what is forbidden, need for what is necessary, would and could to ask politely
a tag that seeks agreement, and a tag that asks you to confirm

units.title: When This Happens
units.context: How things work: what always happens when you do a certain thing. Machines, the body, the weather, the rules of a place.
patterns: if and when for something that is always true: If you press this, the light comes on.
saying what is always true: metal gets hot, the shop opens at nine
it and there when nothing is really doing the action: It takes an hour. There is no signal.

units.title: While I Was
units.context: A longer account of the past: what you were doing when something cut across it, and the detail that makes it clear.
patterns: past forms you cannot work out: taught, threw, spent, hid
one action cutting across another: I was cooking when the power went off.
naming the place and the time inside the sentence: the shop where I bought it
the small words for time, place, position and direction inside one account

units.title: Next Week I Am
units.context: Timetables, bookings and arrangements: several ways to talk about the future, and handing a thing to somebody.
patterns: the timetable present: The train leaves at six. The shop shuts on Sunday.
four ways to say what happens next, and which one to pick
two things after the verb in an instruction: Send me the form. Give it to her.
verbs that take both, with a change of meaning: I stopped to eat, I stopped eating

units.title: More, Less, Fewer
units.context: Measuring and comparing amounts, and naming the things you cannot touch.
patterns: both, all, less, fewer, not as many, not as much
harder, sooner, the earliest: the short forms when you compare the way
by bus, in cash, at once: the small word that comes before the noun
words for what you cannot touch, and two nouns joined into one: kindness, sunshine
units.note: Last unit of Stage 5, so it is a checkpoint: at least four quiz items come from Units 8-13 and the assignment draws on the whole stage.

units.title: Asking Better Questions
units.context: Keeping a conversation going: following something up, suggesting what to do, and talking about people who deal with each other.
patterns: questions that open a subject up: What do you mean by that? How did that go?
what about and how about + a noun or an -ing word to suggest something
verbs with a small word after them: look after, put off, deal with, walk away
as and like to say how: She works as a nurse. It looks like rain.
each other and one another

vocabulary.title: Verbs with a small word after them

units.title: It Is Made Here
units.context: How things are made, grown, sold and mended: describing a process where who does it does not matter.
patterns: is made, are grown, is sold: when who does it does not matter
was delivered, were repaired: the same, once it has already happened
one word for a whole group: a crowd, a flock, a crew
the name of a process: production, delivery, repair

units.title: She Said, He Told Me
units.context: Passing on what somebody said: a message, an instruction, a piece of news you were given.
patterns: said that and told me that: reporting what a person said
reporting an instruction: She told me to wait.
say and tell: only one of them takes a person after it
asking through somebody else: I need you to sign it. I have three calls to make.
words for when it was said: the day before, later that week, straight away

units.title: If and When
units.context: What you will do if something happens: a plan that depends on something else, and what to do when it goes wrong.
patterns: if + present, will + verb: If it rains, I will take the bus.
while, until and as soon as: I will wait until she calls.
saying what will happen after something else does
now, or arranged: the time word is what tells the two apart

units.title: Advice, and Doing It Yourself
units.context: Giving advice and taking it, and doing a thing for yourself rather than having it done for you.
patterns: should and ought to for advice, needn't for what you do not have to do
myself, yourself, himself, herself, ourselves, themselves
responsible for, capable of, keen on: more words that bring their own preposition
in writing, by hand, at last, on purpose: set phrases you learn whole
either, neither, both of, several of, plenty of

units.title: Telling the Whole Story
units.context: Putting the level together: a full account of something that took time, with the people, the detail and what you made of it.
patterns: two actions side by side: while she was driving, I was reading the map
what has only now happened, and what you have done at some point in your life
whose and whom, and extra detail between commas: my manager, who lives nearby, called
three of them in a row, with an -ing or -ed one among them
far, much and well when you compare: it went far better than I expected
units.note: Level capstone AND the last unit of Stage 6. The assignment is a portfolio drawn from at least four units of the level plus recordings, marked on all eight rubric criteria; the quiz spans the whole level and at least four items come from Units 15-19.

levels.label: Level 3 — Threshold
levels.status: Planned — units placed, not yet authored
levels.exitDescriptor: Exits at a secure B1. Can follow the main points of clear speech on familiar matters, deal with most situations that come up while travelling or at work, narrate an event, and write connected text on familiar topics, giving reasons and explanations.

units.title: Telling My Story
units.context: Level 3 opens where most people are asked to speak first: an account of their own life. That is harder than it sounds, because a life is not a sequence of events but a set of turning points, and English marks the difference. This unit gives you the prepositions that follow adjectives, the form for habits that have stopped, and the time expressions that hold a long narrative together. It ends with two personal statements about the same life, one that works and one that does not.
patterns: When the same adjective takes two prepositions
used to: the habit that stopped
I was raised, she was offered: a person at the front
That year I was working nights: the past over a long stretch
Grew up, brought up, settled down: the set a life story runs on
The reason why, and the which that points back

units.title: Saying It Precisely
units.context: Levels 1 and 2 taught you to compare two things and name the best of several. This unit is about precision rather than comparison: the fixed order English uses when several adjectives stack up, the forms for describing how well something is done, and the class of adjectives that already mean extremely and therefore cannot be made stronger. It ends with two product descriptions of the same object, because precision is most visible where somebody is trying to avoid it.
patterns: A well-made chair, a three-year contract: adjectives built from two words
Concerned, demanding, rewarding: the participle adjectives with no obvious pair
Not as good as, much better than: putting a degree on a comparison
Learning a language takes years: -ing at the front of the sentence
In charge of, under pressure, at risk: the preposition carries the meaning

vocabulary.title: Adjectives that cannot be made stronger

units.title: Experience and Change
units.context: This is the largest grammar unit in Level 3 and it fills the biggest gap left by Levels 1 and 2. The present perfect is the form English uses to connect the past to now, and without it you have to work around any statement about experience, duration or change. Four cards: the form, the two words that measure it, the continuous version, and — last, deliberately — the comparison with the past simple you already have.
patterns: One form, three jobs: what the present perfect is actually saying
I have worked there, or I worked there: choosing between the two
Prices are rising: the present continuous for a situation that is changing
Difficult to do, worth doing: what follows an adjective
He does not work as quickly: comparing HOW somebody does it

vocabulary.title: The words that go with the perfect

units.title: Packing More Into a Sentence
units.context: Levels 1 and 2 kept sentences short because you had no way to join a description to a noun. This unit gives you that, and it is the largest single jump in what you can express: relative clauses let one sentence carry what previously took three. It also covers the comma rule, which is not decoration — in a relative clause a comma changes what the sentence means. It ends with a contract clause and its plain-English rewrite.
patterns: What goes before the noun, and what goes after it
In what way? Questions that open an answer up
Could you tell me where it is? The question that stops being a question
Applications are assessed by a panel: the passive of a rule
It is said that: the passive that names nobody at all

units.title: If and Unless
units.context: Conditionals are where English does something that looks illogical until you see the system: it uses a past tense to talk about the present, and a present tense to talk about the future. This unit covers the three you need, in order of distance from reality, plus the one word that catches almost everybody. It ends with an insurance policy, because a policy is nothing but conditions and the whole of it turns on which one you meet.
patterns: Unless, provided, otherwise: saying the condition a different way
No will after if, when or unless
How sure are you? Letting the future form carry your evidence
Most of the people, or most people? The quantifiers Level 2 left out
Decide becomes decision: building the noun you need

units.title: Joining Ideas
units.context: Levels 1 and 2 gave you because and so, which join a reason to a result. This unit gives you the rest of the system, and the practical difficulty is not meaning but punctuation: three groups of connectors mean similar things and attach to sentences in three different ways. Getting that wrong produces the most common punctuation error in English writing. It ends with a paragraph rewritten three times, because connectors are where writing stops being a list of sentences.
patterns: This means that: pointing back at what you just said
However is not but: the word that cannot join two clauses
While it is cheaper, it is slower: contrast that does not start a new sentence
Firstly, subsequently, ultimately: showing the reader the shape
Admittedly, arguably: saying how firmly you mean it

units.title: Opinions and Disagreement
units.context: Disagreeing in a second language is where fluent people most often sound rude by accident, and the reason is almost never grammar. This unit separates fact from opinion, gives you the frames English uses to mark a view as a view, and covers the concession move that makes a disagreement sound considered. It ends with the same disagreement written twice, because the difference between the two is entirely in the framing.
patterns: She asked whether I had finished: reporting a question
Told me to, or asked me to: the difference is who had the power
He claimed, she admitted: the verb that passes judgement
May, might, could: disagreeing without a row
As, therefore, so that, such as: four ways to explain

units.title: Building Words
units.context: This is the unit with the best return on effort in Level 3. Every other unit gives you words; this one gives you a method for producing words you were never taught, and for reading words you have never seen. English builds meaning out of parts, and once you can see the parts, a large vocabulary stops being something you memorise and starts being something you assemble.
patterns: Un-, dis-, in-, im-, il-, ir-: which negative prefix goes where
Six prefixes that change what a word says
Information about, a reason for: the preposition a NOUN brings
Listen to, apply for, depend on: the preposition a VERB brings
Being told, having finished: an -ing form with a voice and a time

units.title: Reporting What People Said
units.context: Reported speech has a reputation for being mechanical, and the mechanism is real: tenses shift back, pronouns change, time words move. But the mechanism is the easy half. The harder half is that the verb you choose to report with — said, claimed, admitted, insisted — tells the reader what you think, and choosing it carelessly is how you take a side without noticing. It ends with one statement reported three ways.
patterns: It had already gone: the tense for the earlier of two past events
He said he had finished: what happens to the tense when you report it
Ordered, urged, advised, permitted: reporting what somebody wanted done
I remember locking it, or I remembered to lock it
In accordance with, with regard to: the formal preposition phrase

vocabulary.title: Reporting verbs that carry a judgement

units.title: The Passive Voice
units.context: The passive is one form applied across every tense you have, so learning it once gives you nine or ten new structures at no extra cost. It is also the most criticised construction in English, usually unfairly — it does three jobs nothing else does, and one job it should not be doing. This unit covers the mechanism, the four reasons to use it, and the fourth of them, which is hiding who acted.
patterns: It is being investigated: the passive while it is still happening
It will be installed: the passive in the future
It must be signed: the passive after a modal
It has been withdrawn: the passive with a perfect
Better, worse, further: the comparatives that do not follow the rule

units.title: Narrating the Past
units.context: Levels 1 and 2 gave you the past simple, which puts events in a line. This unit gives you the two forms that break the line: the past continuous, which sets a scene, and the past perfect, which reaches back behind the story you are telling. Together they let you narrate something complicated without telling it strictly in order. It ends with two witness statements about the same two minutes.
patterns: I have been working here: the form that shows the effort
A number, or a stretch?
It was getting dark and nobody was speaking: setting a scene
Walking into the yard, I saw: the clause with no subject of its own
The worst I have ever seen: when a superlative forces the perfect

units.title: Verb Patterns
units.context: This unit is about what comes after a verb, and it is the area where a learner's English most often stops sounding like a learner's. Some verbs take to, some take -ing, a few take both with different meanings, and several hundred take a small word that changes what they mean entirely. There is no rule for most of it, which is worth saying plainly — but there are patterns, and there is a way of learning the rest that actually works.
patterns: Carry it out, but look into it: which ones split
Carried out, set up, put off: the six a workplace runs on
Everybody has, and somebody left their coat
They helped each other, or they helped themselves?
A lack of, a breakdown in: naming a problem

units.title: Certainty and Possibility
units.context: Levels 1 and 2 used modals to talk about rules — what you have to do, what you must not do. This unit uses the same words for something completely different: working out what is true. Must, might and can't stop being about obligation and start being about deduction, and the same three words then reach backwards to talk about what should have happened. It ends with an investigation report where every conclusion is a deduction.
patterns: If I had the time, I would do it: the unreal present
I wish I knew: complaining without accusing anybody
It must be the seal: working out what is true
I should have checked: regret, and criticism
So as not to, in case: saying what for

units.title: Work, Careers and Applying
units.context: This unit is about the documents and conversations that decide whether you get work. Level 2 Unit 1 gave you the language of describing your work; this one gives you the language of applying for one — the suffixes that name professions, the compressed register of a CV, and the structure that turns an interview answer from a claim into evidence. It ends with the same answer given twice, once as an assertion and once with evidence.
patterns: The company I worked for, or the company for which I worked
Asking for a case, not an opinion
Do you have any questions for us?
Self-motivated, results-driven: what those phrases prove
Twice as many, by far the most: how big was the gap?

units.title: Money, Enterprise and Being a Customer
units.context: Level 2 Units 17 and 18 gave you complain and fault. This unit is the level above: the expressions English uses to measure uncountable things, the vocabulary of price and contract, and the structure of a complaint that gets a remedy rather than an apology. It ends with two complaints about the same problem, one of which was paid and one of which was not.
patterns: I had the boiler serviced: getting somebody else to do it
I got them to replace it: making a person do something
Is deemed, is entitled, is liable: the passive of an agreement
A batch of, a proportion of: measuring what has no number
The more you order, the lower the price

units.title: Media, Technology and Judging a Source
units.context: Unit 9 taught you that the reporting verb carries the writer's judgement. This unit is about the layer above that: attribution that names nobody at all. Sources say, it is understood, critics argue — constructions that sound authoritative and can be entirely empty. It also covers the small words that pair and contrast, the markers that manage a conversation, and a method for judging whether a source is worth believing.
patterns: Sources say: the ladder of who is actually speaking
Minister resigns: how a headline handles time
Council flood defence funding row: reading a chain backwards
Declined to comment: reporting what nobody would say
Actually, mind you, granted: steering mid-sentence

units.title: Environment and Resources
units.context: This unit teaches the register of careful claims. Environmental and scientific writing is full of hedges, causal chains and citations, and all three exist for the same reason: the claims are probabilistic, the causes are indirect, and the evidence belongs to somebody else. Learning to read that register tells you how confident a writer actually is. Learning to write it lets you make claims you can defend.
patterns: This time next year: already under way
Emissions were rising: a measurement that was moving
Is projected to rise: writing about what has not happened
Which in turn: following a cause down the chain
Correlation is not cause

units.title: Writing Formally
units.context: Formality in English is not a single dial. It is several independent choices — vocabulary, contractions, sentence length, how directly you ask — and getting one wrong while getting the others right is what makes a document read oddly. This unit separates them, covers the conventions of the three documents you are most likely to need, and settles a rule about prepositions that has been misapplied for three hundred years.
patterns: The five dials of formality
Your application has been received
Had been forwarded: the order of events in an account
In which case, at which point
Hereby, whereby, pursuant: the words with no plain twin

units.title: Making an Argument
units.context: The last teaching unit of the course, and it assembles most of what came before. An argument has three parts and almost everybody supplies two of them. This unit names the missing one, covers the devices that make an argument persuasive and the line at which they stop being honest, and teaches the move that separates a considered position from a stubborn one — engaging with the strongest version of the other side.
patterns: The conditional that arrives too late
If only: the wish that arrives afterwards
Needn't have, didn't need to
Claim, evidence, warrant: the part nobody writes down
Sheer, outright, downright: the adjectives that only go in front

units.title: Level 3 Capstone — My English Voice
units.context: The last unit of the course. It maps Level 3, assembles it into three pieces of real work, and teaches one thing that is not in any other unit: how to decide what to learn next when nobody is telling you. Level 3 exists in the plan and not yet on the page, so from here you are your own syllabus — and that is a skill rather than a misfortune.
patterns: I had been studying for two years
Four perfect forms, one timeline
Keep up with, catch up on, fall behind
Good at, a gap in, working on
Naming a gap, setting a priority

levels.source: inputs/ehel-english-intensive-source/archive/level-2-b1-2026-08 — the B1 to B1+ course that was Level 2 until 2026-09-12: 20 authored units, 571 words, reviewed and signed off. Benchmark for the rebuild is Interchange 3 (B1 to B1+), whose syllabus matches it closely: relative clauses, gerund phrases as subjects, the past perfect, indirect requests, participles as adjectives.
levels.note: This is the LAST level: the course ends at B1 (see whyTheCourseStopsAtB1). 0876 SPIRALS harder than 0057 did — the present perfect, reported speech, the passive and the conditionals each appear in Stages 7, 8 AND 9 with a wider range each time — so every pattern here must name its INCREMENT, or two units get near-identical card titles and the duplication gate goes red. That cost Level 2 a redraft; see intensive-english/CLAUDE.md.

cefrBands.canDo: Follow the main points of clear speech on familiar matters, describe experiences and events, and write connected text on familiar topics.
Report what others said, describe a process, narrate a sequence of past events, and give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans.
Deal with most situations that arise while travelling or at work, build an argument, judge a source, and write clear connected text on a range of familiar topics.

levels.exitAssessment: A B1 check across the four skills at the end of Unit 20, reported per skill, never as one grade.
levels.contextsNote: Each unit's `context` is the archived course's own overview, repointed at this ladder: it was written when these units were Level 2 sitting on the OLD Level 1 (A1-A2). Capability claims survived that move; the two that named a unit number did not and were corrected against the rebuilt levels. Treat a context as a brief to check, not as verified prose — an author should confirm any prerequisite it claims before relying on it.

teachingLanguage: English. The course is monolingual: it explains English in English, at a level the learner can already read, so it works for a class with no shared first language.
selfTeaching: The course must be completable with no teacher present. Every exercise carries a learner-facing answer key, every task that would need a partner has a solo alternative, every practice is preceded by a worked example, and the learner diagnoses their own errors rather than waiting to be corrected. A teacher, where one exists, is an accelerator and never a dependency.
whyTheCourseStopsAtB1:
Owner, 2026-09-16. Levels 4 (C1) and 5 (C2) were planned and are now dropped, for two reasons that point the same way.

THE DESIGN STOPS FIRST. This course's contract is that every Cambridge objective of a level's stages is placed in exactly one unit and cited by an outcome, and the build fails a unit that does not. That needs a per-stage objective framework. Cambridge's ESL frameworks in that shape are Primary 0057 (Stages 1-6) and Lower Secondary 0876 (Stages 7-9), and they stop there: every framework file in src/curriculum stops at stage 9. Above it the Cambridge ESL route is IGCSE, a qualification syllabus rather than per-stage objectives, so a Level 4 could not be built the way Levels 1 to 3 are. It would need a different framework or none, and a level with no contract is the one thing this plan is designed to prevent.

THE DEMAND IS LOWER, and this was already written down. Level 5's own note said C2 is rarely set as a minimum requirement by anyone — it marks the top of the scale rather than an entry point — so a five-level course may sell on completeness while almost nobody enrols in the top level. That note then named 'Levels 2 and 3 (B1 and B2)' as where the demand sits, which stopped being true when the 2026-09-12 rebuild renumbered the ladder. Read against the ladder as it now stands, the same argument says the demand sits at Level 3 — which is exactly the level that is built, reviewed and waiting on one missing framework file.

A learner who needs B2 or above is past what this course teaches, and is better served by being told so than by an empty level in the list.
